html:
SMTO-API-0003 — Request blocked by safety policy

GUID: ab28f1e3-4f31-4fbc-9ecd-3ae47f085cab
Slug: safety-block
Domain: API · Subsystem: api

What happened

  • SMTO's safety rules stopped one or more actions in your task before they ran, because they could be harmful or aren't allowed here. Those blocked actions were not carried out.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Ask SMTO to reach your goal a different way, for example with a smaller, more specific change that doesn't delete, overwrite, restart or shut anything down. The rule blocks that kind of action itself, so repeating it unchanged, or adding administrator rights (sudo), is blocked again.
  2. If you believe the action should be allowed, ask the person who manages SMTO to review the Unsafe actions setting and the Policy / Permissions rules under Settings › Security. When Unsafe actions is set to Disallow, SMTO blocks risky actions such as deleting or shutting down, and only an administrator should change that.
  3. Before sending the request again, look at the task's steps and note which ones already finished. Other steps in the same task may have done their work, and you don't want to repeat them.

What success looks like

  • The task finishes without a blocked step, using actions your SMTO's rules allow.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO, with a short note on what you were trying to do. Don't try to get around the block by rewording the same risky action or adding administrator rights.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The runtime policy blocked one or more planned actions before execution.

What this means

  • The typed SafetyError family identifies a deterministic policy rejection; its base class does not specify the blocked action or policy rule. Generic API status and exception families establish only their stated boundary. Stronger structured causes take precedence; the original receipt determines whether work started or had effects, and diagnostics add no dispatch or retry.

Why this can happen

  • The typed SafetyError family identifies a deterministic policy rejection; its base class does not specify the blocked action or policy rule.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the actual guard, blocked operation and stage rather than weakening policy or assuming every earlier action was blocked.

How to fix it

  • Identify the blocking rule from the step receipt (runtime_policy_denied with its blocked_reasons, or 'Unsafe actions are disallowed by the global user policy.'). Change the operation to an allowed one, or have an administrator review unsafe_action_policy (Settings › Security › Unsafe actions) and Policy / Permissions; approval or sudo cannot override this denial.
  • Review the specific policy guard and use an allowed authorized action; preserve any earlier execution receipts.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • A supported authorized request passes the exact policy boundary.

What not to do

  • Do not repeatedly submit the same invalid input; correct the named constraint first.

Technical notes

  • Generic API status and exception families establish only their stated boundary. Stronger structured causes take precedence; the original receipt determines whether work started or had effects, and diagnostics add no dispatch or retry.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
